newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico April trade data fail to impress.
newsitem.headline: Mexico April trade data fail to impress.

text.p: April trade data released this week showed a sharp fall in Mexico's trade surplus but analysts said on Tuesday that seasonal distortions meant the numbers should not be seen in isolation.

Mexico's preliminary April trade surplus came in at $109 million, a sharp fall from March's downwardly revised $611 million and February's $383 million. The data put some pressure on the peso on Monday amid a possibly faster than expected move towards a trade deficit.
But analysts said a number of public holidays distorted the April data, which should be viewed together with March's numbers for a more accurate view.

"If you look at the trend line, you are seeing some deterioriation on the trade side, but it is not nearly as serious as the April preliminary trade report viewed in isolation," said Gray Newman, chief economist for Mexico at HSBC James Capel here. Averaging the two months to iron out the holiday distortions, he said the surplus was closer to $360 million. Surpluses ranged from $200 milllion to $800 million monthly during 1996.
Economists at IDEA said seasonally adjusted trade surpluses averaged $350 million in the first quarter, adding it was too soon to say whether April's figure was the start of a new trend.
But they added that even when the numbers are averaged out, they suggest the trade surplus could turn into a deficit faster than the year-end timeframe predicted.

"Even averaging the seasonally adjusted March and April results to remove the working day distortion leaves a somewhat worrisome picture of flat monthly trade balances as early as end-Q2," said one analyst.

Many analysts, breaking down the trade figures, were surprised by strength in import growth, with consumer and capital goods shooting up about 53 percent over the year- earlier period -- their strongest performance since October 1986.
Sergio Martin, chief economist for Mexico at ING Barings here, said they fuelled hopes that the long-awaited upturn in domestic consumption may be on its way at last.
"It appears we are seeing some recovery in domestic demand," added Scott Grimberg, Latin American analyst at MMS in New York.
Newman said a declining trade surplus was not in itself a negative given that Mexico's current stage of economic development required more capital inflows from abroad.
"But if we have a deterioriation in the trade figures we hope it will be accompanied by a rebound in the domestic economy too; that should come later in the year," he added.

However, hopes that stronger imports suggested a recovery in domestic demand were dampened somewhat by disappointing numbers on Monday from Mexico's retailers association ANCTAD, which showed April supermarket sales dropping 4.0 percent.
Gerardo Copca, economist at Valores Finamex, said the situation in the sector remains difficult.

"Consumer prices continue to rise while salaries stagnate, though some recovery in employment is moderating the bad news," he said in a report, adding the majority of consumers remain focused on low-priced articles.

Nor did a rise in department store sales, which posted 3.2 percent growth in April, outweigh the poor showing on the supermarket front. That rise has to be seen in the light of a very low base of comparison due to the weak 1995 recession year, Copca said.
